title: Parmanand: hear, then do
hook: what use is hearing holy stories if devotion doesn't follow (Sarang, Parmanand, ang 1253)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramanand: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love? Today, a hard question about listening.

A cookbook on the nightstand, its pages soft from reading in bed. Every recipe known by heart. The oven has never been switched on. Reading about bread is a real pleasure. It just doesn't feed anybody. In Raag Sarang, on Ang 1253 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Parmanand turns to someone who has heard every holy story there is, and asks a blunt question: so what did all that listening do?
screen: `A COOKBOOK READ IN BED.` → `THE OVEN NEVER ON.` → `WHAT DID THE LISTENING DO?`

segments.voice: Parmanand is one of the Bhagats, the devotees outside the line of the Gurus whose words sit in the Granth. The Granth tells almost nothing about his life; what it keeps is his hymn. It opens, in paraphrase: man, what have you gained by hearing the Puranas? Steady devotion never rose up in you, and you gave nothing to the hungry. The Puranas are old books of sacred stories, gods and kings and devotees, read aloud and loved. Parmanand isn't sneering at the stories. He's looking at the listener who walks away from them unchanged. Then he names what didn't move: lust and anger and greed are still there, and the mouth still hasn't stopped speaking ill of others. The stories went in at the ears and stopped. Look at his test. Not how many stories you know, or how beautifully you retell them. Two plain questions: did devotion grow, and did the hungry get fed? A heart turned toward God, and a hand turned toward the person in front of you, named side by side, and the listener has neither. The Granth keeps that question in his own voice. Which is a little awkward for a lesson like this one, since a lesson is also something heard. A story heard is a seed in a pocket. Parmanand's question is whether it ever goes into the ground.
screen: `WHAT DID HEARING THE PURANAS GAIN YOU?` · `NOT THE STORIES: THE UNCHANGED LISTENER.` · `TWO TESTS: DEVOTION, AND THE HUNGRY FED.` · `A SEED IN A POCKET.` · then, large: `HEAR, THEN DO.`

segments.voice: Bring back one story from this path lately: Sain offering his work, Pipa finding the temple in the body, Ramanand at home in a house colored with love. Hold it, and ask what it would look like as one small thing done, a meal shared, a sharp word left unsaid, until it feels like a plan instead of a wish. If you pray, Waheguru can go with each breath out.
Parmanand. A Bhagat whose hymn in Raag Sarang asks what the hearing was for, if devotion never grew and the hungry went unfed.
Your line: hear, then do. Listening is the start, not the finish. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Parmanand's hymn in Raag Sarang is sung in kirtan like other Gurbani, and Sikhs read it as a call to let what is heard in the gurdwara change how they live and give.
